title: Week 7 · Lesson 21: Infectious Disease & Sepsis — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 7 — Lesson 21: Infectious Disease & Sepsis

FNP-level goal: Identify the likely source and severity of infection, distinguish localized disease from infection-associated organ dysfunction, choose a safe diagnostic and disposition pathway, apply antimicrobial-stewardship reasoning, and recognize when source control or emergency care is needed.

Learning Objectives

  • Use host factors, syndrome, vital signs, and examination findings to stratify infection severity.
  • Differentiate colonization, contamination, inflammation, and clinically important infection.
  • Recognize sepsis as infection-associated life-threatening organ dysfunction and identify emergency red flags.
  • Build focused differentials for respiratory, urinary, skin/soft-tissue, abdominal, and device-related presentations.
  • Choose tests that answer a clinical question and apply safe antimicrobial and referral principles.

Part 1 — The FNP Infection Framework

Do not begin with “Which antibiotic should I prescribe?” Begin with: Is this truly an infection? Where is the source? How sick is the patient? What host factors change risk? Does this patient need a procedure, emergency evaluation, or a higher level of care?

Infectious presentations reflect an interaction among pathogen, host, and anatomic site. The same organism can cause mild disease in one person and life-threatening disease in another because of age, pregnancy, immune suppression, diabetes, CKD, liver disease, malignancy, implanted devices, vascular disease, medication exposures, or delayed presentation.

Source + host vulnerability + physiologic response + trajectory = disposition.

Part 2 — Infection Is Not the Same as Inflammation

Inflammation is a host response that can occur with infection, ischemia, autoimmune disease, crystal arthritis, trauma, malignancy, medication reactions, or thrombosis. Fever, leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, tachycardia, and malaise are clues; none alone proves a bacterial infection.

Colonization means organisms are present without tissue invasion or illness. Contamination means a specimen contains organisms introduced during collection or handling. Infection requires a compatible syndrome plus evidence that a pathogen is causing clinically meaningful disease.

FNP reasoning: do not treat a laboratory result in isolation. Ask whether the symptoms, examination, specimen quality, and pretest probability support the diagnosis.

Part 3 — Localized Disease Versus Systemic Illness

A localized infection may cause pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, drainage, cough, dysuria, or focal tenderness while vital signs and organ function remain stable. Systemic illness may produce fever or hypothermia, rigors, tachycardia, tachypnea, weakness, nausea, altered mentation, reduced urine output, hypotension, hypoxemia, or rapidly worsening pain.

Temperature is not a severity scale. Older adults, people with immune suppression, and patients using antipyretics may have serious infection without a high fever. Conversely, fever by itself does not establish sepsis.

Part 4 — Sepsis: The Clinical Concept

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. It is not synonymous with infection, bacteremia, fever, or a positive culture. In practice, recognize infection plus evidence that perfusion, respiratory function, mentation, renal function, circulation, or another organ system may be failing.

Concerning findings include new confusion, hypotension, cool or clammy skin, weak pulse, tachypnea or increased work of breathing, hypoxemia, oliguria, cyanosis, mottling, severe weakness, or rapid deterioration. Screening tools can organize thinking, but no score replaces clinical judgment. When infection and possible organ dysfunction coexist, do not continue a prolonged outpatient workup: activate the local emergency pathway and give a concise handoff.

Part 5 — Why Sepsis Deteriorates

Severe infection can trigger dysregulated inflammatory, endothelial, coagulation, and microcirculatory responses. Vasodilation and capillary leak can reduce effective circulating volume; endothelial injury and microvascular dysfunction can impair oxygen delivery even before blood pressure falls markedly.

Infection → dysregulated host response → vasodilation/capillary leak/microcirculatory dysfunction → impaired tissue perfusion → cellular stress and organ dysfunction.

Compensatory tachycardia may initially preserve cardiac output. As illness progresses, hypotension, altered mental status, kidney injury, hypoxemia, or mottled skin may appear. These are potential signals of failing oxygen delivery, not merely abnormal numbers.

Part 6 — Focused History: Find the Source and the Clock

Ask about onset, sequence, speed of progression, focal symptoms, recent procedures, wounds, travel, animal or water exposure, sexual history when relevant, sick contacts, food exposures, recent hospitalization, prior culture results, recent antimicrobial use, and implanted devices.

  • Respiratory: cough, sputum, pleuritic pain, dyspnea, aspiration risk, hypoxemia.
  • Urinary: dysuria, urgency, flank pain, fever, retention, catheter, stone history, pregnancy.
  • Skin/soft tissue: portal of entry, drainage, fluctuance, rapid spread, disproportionate pain, bite, injection, diabetic foot wound.
  • Abdominal: pain location, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, prior surgery, obstruction symptoms.
  • Neurologic: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, focal deficit, seizure, new confusion.

A stable three-day cough and a patient whose erythema, pain, tachycardia, and weakness worsened over hours are different clinical problems.

Part 7 — Examination and Perfusion Assessment

Start with general appearance, mental status, airway, respiratory effort, oxygenation, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, and pain. Repeat abnormal vital signs rather than dismissing one value. Examine the suspected source and assess for complications.

Look for perfusion clues: capillary refill trend, skin temperature/color, pulse quality, urine output history, mucous membranes, mental status, and ability to speak or ambulate. Disproportionate pain, rapidly advancing erythema, bullae, skin anesthesia, crepitus, necrosis, hypotension, or toxic appearance are not routine cellulitis findings. They warrant immediate escalation for possible deep or necrotizing infection.

Part 8 — Differential Diagnosis: Resist Premature Closure

Fever plus dyspnea may be pneumonia, viral illness, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, asthma/COPD exacerbation, acute coronary syndrome, or another process. Dysuria may reflect cystitis, pyelonephritis, STI/urethritis, vaginitis, stone disease, retention, or noninfectious bladder pain.

A red, swollen leg may be cellulitis, venous stasis dermatitis, DVT, contact dermatitis, gout, trauma, or an abscess. Abdominal pain with systemic findings may reflect biliary disease, pancreatitis, appendicitis, obstruction, ischemia, urinary infection, pelvic pathology, or gastroenteritis. Ask: Does the proposed infection explain the entire presentation, including the vital signs and severity?

Part 9 — Tests Should Answer a Question

Order testing when it changes diagnosis, disposition, treatment, or monitoring. In a stable uncomplicated syndrome with clear diagnostic criteria, extensive testing may add little. In a high-risk or systemically ill patient, targeted testing can identify organ dysfunction, guide therapy, and clarify the source.

Depending on the presentation, evaluation may include a properly collected urinalysis/culture, targeted respiratory testing, CBC, metabolic panel, pregnancy test when relevant, blood cultures, lactate, blood gas, chest imaging, ECG, ultrasound, CT, or source-directed cultures. In suspected sepsis, emergency clinicians coordinate time-sensitive testing and treatment; cultures are valuable when obtainable without delaying urgently needed care.

Interpret tests with the bedside picture. A contaminated urine specimen, incidental radiographic finding, or one culture result may not explain illness. Conversely, normal early testing does not overrule a concerning trajectory.

Part 10 — Microbiology and Specimen Quality

A culture is only as useful as the specimen. Teach collection technique, document antimicrobial exposure, and obtain material from the most informative source when feasible. Superficial swabs may not represent deep tissue infection. A positive result should fit the patient’s syndrome.

When culture and susceptibility results return, review deliberately: Does the organism fit? Is the prescribed agent active? Can therapy be narrowed, stopped, changed, or converted appropriately according to current local guidance and the patient’s condition?

Part 11 — Antimicrobial Stewardship Is Patient Safety

Antibiotics do not treat viral illness and do not substitute for a diagnosis. Unnecessary exposure can cause allergic reactions, drug interactions, adverse effects, C. difficile infection, and selection of resistant organisms.

Before prescribing, ask:

  1. Is a bacterial syndrome likely enough to benefit from an antimicrobial?
  2. What site and likely pathogens are being targeted?
  3. Is the patient stable for outpatient treatment?
  4. What allergy history, prior cultures, recent antibiotics, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy/lactation considerations, drug interactions, and immune status matter?
  5. What current local and national guidance applies?
  6. What follow-up finding would require reassessment or escalation?

When treatment is indicated, use the narrowest effective evidence-based regimen and duration consistent with current guidance, local susceptibility patterns, and the patient’s syndrome. Reassess diagnosis and response rather than automatically extending or broadening therapy.

Part 12 — Source Control Changes the Plan

Some infections cannot resolve with antimicrobials alone. An abscess may require incision and drainage; an infected joint may require urgent aspiration/drainage; an obstructed infected urinary or biliary system may require urgent decompression; devitalized tissue may require surgery; and an infected device may need removal or specialist management.

Failure to improve is diagnostic information. Reconsider resistant or incorrect organism coverage, poor adherence or absorption, inadequate dosing for organ function, an undrained collection, obstruction, deep infection, vascular insufficiency, an incorrect diagnosis, or a new complication.

Part 13 — Common High-Risk Presentations

Urinary symptoms

Differentiate lower urinary symptoms from pyelonephritis or complicated infection. Fever, flank pain, vomiting, systemic illness, pregnancy, obstruction, immune compromise, catheter use, or inability to take oral fluids changes risk and may change disposition. Do not equate bacteriuria alone with symptomatic UTI.

Skin and soft-tissue infection

Decide whether the dominant process is diffuse cellulitis, a drainable abscess, ulcer infection, bite-related infection, ischemic tissue, or another mimic. In diabetes or peripheral arterial disease, assess depth, necrosis, neuropathy, perfusion, and bone-involvement risk. Rapid progression or systemic toxicity is an emergency.

Respiratory symptoms

Assess oxygenation, respiratory effort, focal lung findings, comorbid cardiopulmonary disease, aspiration risk, and noninfectious causes. A patient with tachypnea, hypoxemia, confusion, or inability to maintain oral intake needs more than a routine “bronchitis” plan.

Diarrhea after antibiotics or healthcare exposure

Consider medication adverse effects and C. difficile when compatible diarrhea follows antimicrobial exposure or healthcare contact. Severe abdominal pain, dehydration, fever, ileus, or toxic appearance requires urgent evaluation.

Part 14 — Special Populations

Older adults: may present with functional decline, delirium, falls, anorexia, or weakness rather than fever. Seek a compatible source; do not diagnose UTI solely from a positive urine test without symptoms or an appropriate syndrome.

Pregnancy: physiologic changes and fetal considerations alter differential diagnosis, testing, medication selection, and referral threshold. Fever, flank pain, dehydration, respiratory compromise, or abdominal/pelvic pain deserve a lower threshold for escalation.

Immunocompromised patients: may have muted signs and a broader pathogen differential. Neutropenia, transplant-related immunosuppression, advanced HIV, biologic therapy, chemotherapy, or high-dose corticosteroids lower the threshold for urgent evaluation and specialist input.

Diabetes, CKD, liver disease, and vascular disease: increase the risk of severe infection, impaired healing, medication toxicity, and complications; they also affect outpatient eligibility and antimicrobial selection.

Part 15 — Outpatient Versus Emergency Disposition

Outpatient management is reasonable only when the patient is clinically stable, has a plausible uncomplicated syndrome, can obtain and take treatment, has reliable follow-up, understands safety-net instructions, and has no red flags or high-risk features requiring higher-level care.

Emergency evaluation is appropriate for:

  • suspected sepsis or shock; new altered mental status; persistent hypotension; hypoxemia; severe tachypnea; or poor perfusion;
  • rapidly progressive pain, swelling, erythema, necrosis, crepitus, bullae, or pain out of proportion;
  • inability to maintain hydration or oral therapy, persistent vomiting, or severe weakness;
  • possible meningitis, septic arthritis, deep-space infection, infected obstruction, acute abdomen, or acute pulmonary compromise;
  • high-risk host factors plus concerning symptoms or an unreliable outpatient safety plan.

In a handoff, communicate the suspected source, onset and trajectory, current and repeat vital signs, oxygen requirement, mental status, high-risk conditions, therapies already given, allergies, and why organ dysfunction or a procedure may be needed.

Part 16 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 1: Worsening Cellulitis

A 58-year-old patient with diabetes presents with rapidly expanding leg erythema, severe pain, HR 122, BP 92/58, confusion, and reduced urine output. Do not frame this as routine antibiotic failure.

Mechanism: skin/soft-tissue infection plus systemic deterioration suggests infection-associated circulatory and renal dysfunction.

FNP decision: emergency evaluation now; communicate concern for sepsis and possible deep infection/source-control need. Do not delay transfer for an extended clinic workup.

Part 17 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 2: Dysuria Is Not Always Simple Cystitis

A 31-year-old pregnant patient has dysuria, fever, vomiting, flank pain, and tachycardia. The differential includes upper urinary tract infection and complications; pregnancy raises the stakes.

FNP decision: assess stability, hydration, and systemic involvement; arrange urgent higher-level evaluation rather than treating this as uncomplicated outpatient cystitis.

Part 18 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 3: Positive Test, Wrong Diagnosis

An 82-year-old with chronic urinary colonization has a positive urine culture obtained during evaluation for unilateral leg swelling. She has no dysuria, fever, suprapubic pain, flank pain, or systemic instability.

FNP reasoning: a positive culture alone does not prove symptomatic UTI. Continue evaluating the leg swelling, including vascular and noninfectious causes, and avoid reflex antimicrobial treatment without a compatible syndrome.

Part 19 — Follow-Up and Safety-Netting

A safe plan states what improvement should look like, when to reassess, how results will be reviewed, and which symptoms require immediate emergency care. Give clear return precautions: worsening shortness of breath, persistent vomiting, confusion, fainting, new chest pain, rapidly spreading redness, inability to urinate, reduced urine output, new severe pain, or any rapid decline.

Follow-up is part of antimicrobial stewardship, diagnostic safety, and infection management. A patient who is not improving as expected needs reassessment of diagnosis, source control, adherence, resistance, complications, and disposition.

FNP High-Yield Framework

1. Identify: likely source, pathogen category, and host vulnerability.
2. Assess severity: appearance, repeated vital signs, oxygenation, perfusion, mentation, urine output, and trajectory.
3. Consider mimics: inflammation and abnormal tests do not automatically equal bacterial infection.
4. Test with purpose: obtain the specimen or study that changes management.
5. Treat safely: use current evidence/local guidance, patient-specific factors, and the narrowest effective therapy when indicated.
6. Seek source control: abscess, obstruction, device, devitalized tissue, or deep infection may require a procedure.
7. Escalate: infection plus possible organ dysfunction, instability, or a high-risk presentation is an emergency problem.
